```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

set.seed(258)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

plot_cols <- list(
  teal        = "#00695c",
  teal_dark   = "#004d40",
  teal_light  = "#e0f2f1",
  blue        = "#c8e6f3",
  blue_soft   = "#eef8fb",
  grey        = "#f5f6f7",
  yellow      = "#fff8e1",
  orange      = "#f9a825",
  red         = "#c62828",
  text        = "#2f3437",
  muted       = "#667174",
  border      = "#d8dee2",
  code        = "#f3f4f5",
  white       = "#ffffff"
)

plotly_anova_layout <- function(
  p,
  title = NULL,
  x_title = NULL,
  y_title = NULL,
  height = 360,
  margin = list(l = 70, r = 24, t = 58, b = 64)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 16), x = 0.02),
      height = height,
      margin = margin,
      xaxis = list(
        title = x_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = y_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      dragmode = FALSE,
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white",
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE,
      doubleClick = FALSE,
      responsive = FALSE
    )
}
```

});

---

## Why ANOVA?

::: {.defbox}
**Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)** is used to compare several population means.

Suppose we have $k$ groups, usually with $k \ge 3$.
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Question</span>

Do all groups have the same population mean?
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Null hypothesis</span>

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Alternative</span>

$$
H_a:\text{at least one }\mu_j\text{ is different}
$$
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
ANOVA starts with one global test. If the global test rejects, then pairwise comparisons can ask which means differ.
:::

---

## One-Factor ANOVA Model

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
The textbook model is:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

where $Y_{ij}$ is observation $j$ in group $i$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Meaning</span>

- $\mu$: overall mean
- $\tau_i$: treatment-specific effect
- $\epsilon_{ij}$: random error term
- $\mu+\tau_i$: group mean
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
Equivalent form:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

where $\mu_i$ is the population mean for group $i$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Every observation in the same group is assigned the same group mean, plus random error.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Data Structure and Notation

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
| Group 1 | Group 2 | $\cdots$ | Group $k$ |
|---:|---:|:---:|---:|
| $X_{11}$ | $X_{21}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k1}$ |
| $X_{12}$ | $X_{22}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k2}$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $X_{1n_1}$ | $X_{2n_2}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{kn_k}$ |
| $\bar X_1$ | $\bar X_2$ | $\cdots$ | $\bar X_k$ |
| $S_1^2$ | $S_2^2$ | $\cdots$ | $S_k^2$ |
| $n_1$ | $n_2$ | $\cdots$ | $n_k$ |
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Notation</span>

- $\bar X_i$: sample mean of group $i$
- $S_i^2$: sample variance of group $i$
- $n_i$: sample size of group $i$
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Total sample size:

$$
n=n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_k
$$

Overall sample mean:

$$
\bar X=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}X_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i\bar X_i
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## ANOVA as a Prediction Problem

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
ANOVA can be understood as comparing two prediction rules.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Ignore group information</span>

Predict every observation using the overall mean:

$$
\bar X
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Use group information</span>

Predict observation $j$ in group $i$ using the group mean:

$$
\bar X_i
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
If group means improve prediction by a lot compared with the within-group noise, the ANOVA $F$ statistic becomes large.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Sources of Variation

::: {.defbox}
ANOVA works by splitting variation into two pieces: variation **within** groups and variation **between** groups.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Within groups: error variation</span>

$$
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
$$

This is residual variation inside the groups.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Between groups: treatment variation</span>

$$
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
$$

This captures how group means differ from the overall mean.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The ANOVA $F$ statistic becomes large when between-group variation is large relative to within-group error variation.
:::

---

## Total Variation and Decomposition

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
Total variation:

$$
SSTotal=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decomposition identity</span>

$$
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
ANOVA compares:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text{between-group variation}\\[2pt]
&\qquad\quad \text{vs.}\\[2pt]
&\text{within-group variation}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
If group means are close together, $SSTr$ is small.

If at least one group mean is far away, $SSTr$ becomes larger.
:::
:::
::::

---

## The ANOVA Table

| Source | df | SS | MS | F-statistic |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | $k-1$ | $SSTr$ | $MSTr=\dfrac{SSTr}{k-1}$ | $F^*=\dfrac{MSTr}{MSE}$ |
| Error | $n-k$ | $SSE$ | $MSE=\dfrac{SSE}{n-k}$ |  |
| Total | $n-1$ | $SSTotal$ |  |  |

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Mean square rule</span>

$$
MS=\frac{SS}{df}
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The $F$ statistic compares treatment variation per degree of freedom with error variation per degree of freedom.
:::

---

## ANOVA Hypothesis Test

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
Hypotheses:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one }\mu_j\text{ is different}
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Test statistic</span>

$$
F^*=
\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{SSTr/(k-1)}{SSE/(n-k)}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
Under $H_0$:

$$
F^* \sim F_{k-1,n-k}
$$

The numerator degrees of freedom are $k-1$.

The denominator degrees of freedom are $n-k$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The ANOVA p-value is the area to the **right** of $F^*$, because large $F$ values mean group means differ more than expected from random error alone.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions of ANOVA

::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.72em; line-height: 1.24; padding: 15px 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>

<ul class="assumption-list" style="gap: 10px;">
  <li>Observations are independent.</li>
  <li>Error terms, or residuals, are Normal.</li>
  <li>All groups have the same population variance: $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2=\sigma^2$.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
The common variance is estimated using the Mean Squared Error from ANOVA:

$$
\hat\sigma^2=MSE
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
This is why the denominator of the $F$ statistic is $MSE$: it estimates the shared within-group variance.
:::

---

## ANOVA P-value Visual

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Right-tail reference distribution</span>

For $k=3$ groups and $n=18$ observations:

$$
df_1=k-1=2,
\qquad
df_2=n-k=15
$$

The shaded region is:

$$
P(F_{2,15}\ge F^*)
$$

In R, this is calculated with `lower.tail = FALSE`.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 8, length.out = 500)
fstar <- 5.85
f_df <- data.frame(x = x, density = stats::df(x, df1 = 2, df2 = 15))
shade_df <- f_df |> filter(x >= fstar)

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = f_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~density,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$text, width = 2.6),
    hovertemplate = "F = %{x:.2f}<br>Density = %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    data = shade_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~density,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    fill = "tozeroy",
    fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.38)",
    line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.90)", width = 1.5),
    hovertemplate = "p-value tail<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  layout(
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line",
      x0 = fstar,
      x1 = fstar,
      y0 = 0,
      y1 = max(f_df$density) * 0.92,
      line = list(color = plot_cols$teal_dark, width = 2.4, dash = "dash")
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = fstar + 0.55,
      y = max(f_df$density) * 0.55,
      text = "p-value",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      font = list(size = 13, color = plot_cols$text)
    ))
  ) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "Right-tail p-value for ANOVA",
    x_title = "F",
    y_title = "Density",
    height = 345
  )
```
:::
::::

## Example: Campus Café Pickup Systems {.cafe-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.43fr 0.57fr; gap: 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="font-size: 0.62em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A campus café wants to compare **three pickup systems** used during the same lunch rush period:

- mobile order,
- kiosk order,
- counter order.

For each system, the café records the number of minutes from **order confirmation to pickup**.

We want to know whether the **population mean pickup time** is the same for all three systems.

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 12px; margin-bottom: 12px;">

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one mean pickup time differs}
$$

</div>

Use a **one-way ANOVA at the 5% level**.
:::

::: {.col style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; gap: 16px;"}

::: {.stat-card style="font-size: 0.55em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Observed data</span>

| Mobile order | Kiosk order | Counter order |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 5.0 | 6.5 | 7.8 |
| 6.0 | 6.5 | 8.8 |
| 7.0 | 8.5 | 9.8 |
| 7.0 | 9.5 | 10.6 |
| 8.0 | 9.5 | 11.8 |
| 9.0 | 10.5 | 12.4 |
:::

::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.22; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA setup</span>

The explanatory variable is the **pickup system**.

The response variable is **pickup wait time**.

There are $k=3$ groups and $n=18$ observations.

Each system has $n_i=6$ wait-time measurements.
:::

:::

::::

---

## Campus Café: ANOVA Result {.cafe-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.60fr 0.40fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation table</span>

The grand mean is $\bar{x}=8.57$. The final two columns give the pieces that add to $SSE$ and $SSTr$.

| System | $n_i$ | $\bar{x}_i$ | $s_i^2$ | $(n_i-1)s_i^2$ | $n_i(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Mobile | 6 | 7.00 | 2.00 | 10.00 | 14.73 |
| Kiosk | 6 | 8.50 | 2.80 | 14.00 | 0.03 |
| Counter | 6 | 10.20 | 3.09 | 15.44 | 16.01 |
| **Totals** | **18** |  |  | **39.44** | **30.76** |

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 1.08em; margin-top: 12px;">

$$
SSE=39.44,
\qquad
SSTr=30.76,
\qquad
SSTotal=70.20
$$

</div>
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.56em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 15px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA table</span>

| Source | df | SS | MS | F | p-value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | 2 | 30.76 | 15.38 | 5.85 | 0.0132 |
| Error | 15 | 39.44 | 2.63 |  |  |
| Total | 17 | 70.20 |  |  |  |

$$
MSTr=\frac{30.76}{2}=15.38
$$

$$
MSE=\frac{39.44}{15}=2.63
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{15.38}{2.63}=5.85
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.21; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>

Since $p=0.0132<0.05$, reject $H_0$.

There is evidence that **not all pickup systems** have the same population mean pickup wait time.

The ANOVA test tells us that at least one system has a different mean. It does **not** tell us which systems differ.
:::

::::

## Visual: Campus Café Pickup Systems

```{r}
#| echo: false
cafe <- data.frame(
  wait_time = c(5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0,
                6.5, 6.5, 8.5, 9.5, 9.5, 10.5,
                7.8, 8.8, 9.8, 10.6, 11.8, 12.4),
  system = factor(rep(c("Mobile order", "Kiosk order", "Counter order"), each = 6),
                  levels = c("Mobile order", "Kiosk order", "Counter order"))
)

cafe_means <- cafe |>
  group_by(system) |>
  summarise(mean_wait = mean(wait_time), .groups = "drop")

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = cafe,
    x = ~system,
    y = ~wait_time,
    type = "box",
    name = "",
    boxpoints = FALSE,
    whiskerwidth = 0.55,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,77,64,0.88)", width = 2.1),
    fillcolor = "rgba(200,230,243,0.40)",
    hovertemplate = "System: %{x}<br>Wait time: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_markers(
    data = cafe_means,
    x = ~system,
    y = ~mean_wait,
    marker = list(size = 9, color = plot_cols$red, symbol = "circle",
                  line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = "System: %{x}<br>Mean wait: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "Pickup wait times by ordering system",
    x_title = "Ordering system",
    y_title = "Wait time (minutes)",
    height = 390,
    margin = list(l = 76, r = 25, t = 60, b = 70)
  ) |>
  layout(
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Wait time (minutes)",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 5,
      dtick = 1,
      range = c(4.6, 12.8)
    )
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.68em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-top: 10px;"}
The **red dots** show the group means. Counter order is centered higher than the other systems, which is why the ANOVA table gives a small p-value.
:::

## Example: Short-Form Video Edit Styles {.video-example}

<span class="label">Problem</span>

A creator wants to compare **four video edit styles** used on comparable short videos from the same account:

- clean cut,
- captions-first,
- meme overlay,
- story hook.

For each video, the creator records the **viewer watch time** in seconds.

We want to know whether the **population mean watch time** is the same for all four edit styles.

<div class="calc-left" style="font-size: 0.95em; margin-top: 12px; margin-bottom: 12px;">

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3=\mu_4
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one mean watch time differs}
$$

</div>

Use a **one-way ANOVA at the 5% level**.
:::

::: {.col style="display:grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr; gap: 16px;"}

::: {.stat-card style="font-size: 0.53em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 13px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Observed data</span>

| Clean cut | Captions-first | Meme overlay | Story hook |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | 39 | 35 | 46 |
| 36 | 39 | 40 | 49 |
| 38 | 44 | 41 | 52 |
| 40 | 49 | 42 | 55 |
| 44 | 49 | 47 | 58 |
:::

::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.22; padding: 17px 19px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA setup</span>

The explanatory variable is the **edit style**.

The response variable is **viewer watch time**.

There are $k=4$ groups and $n=20$ observations.

Each edit style has $n_i=5$ watch-time measurements.
:::

:::

## What If ANOVA Rejects?

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
ANOVA's alternative is broad:

$$
H_a:\text{at least one mean is different}
$$

So after rejecting $H_0$, we still need to ask:

**Which mean or means are different?**
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Pairwise comparisons</span>

Compare the means in pairs.

For three groups:

- $\mu_1$ vs. $\mu_2$
- $\mu_1$ vs. $\mu_3$
- $\mu_2$ vs. $\mu_3$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Number of pairwise comparisons:

$$
m=\binom{k}{2}
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Pairwise Confidence Intervals

::: {.defbox}
For comparing two group means after ANOVA, use intervals for:

$$
\mu_i-\mu_j
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Fisher's LSD</span>

$$
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)
\pm
t_{n-k,\alpha/2}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

More power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Bonferroni</span>

$$
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)
\pm
t_{n-k,\alpha/(2m)}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

where $m=\binom{k}{2}$.
:::
::::

---

## Fisher LSD vs. Bonferroni

| Method | What it does | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Fisher LSD | Uses ordinary pairwise intervals after ANOVA | Higher power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error |
| Bonferroni | Adjusts each interval for the number of comparisons | Controls experiment-wise Type I error, but intervals are wider |

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Least significant difference</span>

$$
LSD=
t_{\alpha/2,v}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

Conclude two means differ if:

$$
|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|>LSD
$$
:::

## Example: Badminton Drill Accuracy Scores {.badminton-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.42fr 0.58fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 12px 16px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.52em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 12px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A badminton coach compares three drill programs for improving serve-target accuracy.

After two months, each player completes the same accuracy test out of 40.

| Static targets | Footwork + serve | Coach-fed targets |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 19 | 24 | 26 |
| 20 | 25 | 27 |
| 21 | 26 | 28 |
| 23 | 28 | 29 |
| 24 | 29 | 30 |
| 25 | 30 | 31 |

ANOVA rejects $H_0$. Which drill programs differ?
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.46em; line-height: 1.02; padding: 12px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculations</span>

$$
\bar{x}_1=22,
\qquad
\bar{x}_2=27,
\qquad
\bar{x}_3=28.5,
\qquad
\bar{x}=25.83
$$

| Drill program | $n_i$ | $\bar{x}_i$ | $s_i^2$ | $(n_i-1)s_i^2$ | $n_i(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x})^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Static targets | 6 | 22.00 | 5.60 | 28.00 | 88.17 |
| Footwork + serve | 6 | 27.00 | 5.60 | 28.00 | 8.17 |
| Coach-fed targets | 6 | 28.50 | 3.50 | 17.50 | 42.67 |
| **Totals** | **18** |  |  | **73.50** | **139.00** |

$$
SSE=73.50,
\qquad
SSTr=139.00
$$

$$
MSE=\frac{SSE}{n-k}
=
\frac{73.50}{18-3}
=
4.90
$$

$$
MSTr=\frac{SSTr}{k-1}
=
\frac{139.00}{3-1}
=
69.50
$$

$$
F^*
=
\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{69.50}{4.90}
=
14.18
$$

$$
p\approx0.00035
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.52em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 12px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni setup</span>

There are

$$
m=\binom{3}{2}=3
$$

pairwise comparisons.

Compare:

<span style="font-size: 0.94em;">
Static vs Footwork, Static vs Coach-fed, and Footwork vs Coach-fed.
</span>

Use the pooled ANOVA estimate $MSE=4.90$ for the pairwise intervals.
:::

::::

---

## Example: Badminton Drill Accuracy Scores {.badminton-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.42fr 0.58fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 12px 16px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1 / span 2; font-size: 0.52em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 12px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Problem</span>

A badminton coach compares three drill programs for improving serve-target accuracy.

After two months, each player completes the same accuracy test out of 40.

| Static targets | Footwork + serve | Coach-fed targets |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 19 | 24 | 26 |
| 20 | 25 | 27 |
| 21 | 26 | 28 |
| 23 | 28 | 29 |
| 24 | 29 | 30 |
| 25 | 30 | 31 |

ANOVA rejects $H_0$. Which drill programs differ?
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Given from ANOVA</span>

Since ANOVA rejects $H_0$, we continue to pairwise comparisons.

Use the ANOVA error estimate:

$$
MSE=4.90,
\qquad
v=n-k=18-3=15
$$

The group means are:

$$
\bar{x}_{Static}=22,
\qquad
\bar{x}_{Footwork}=27,
\qquad
\bar{x}_{Coach}=28.5
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni setup</span>

There are

$$
m=\binom{3}{2}=3
$$

pairwise comparisons:

- Static vs Footwork
- Static vs Coach-fed
- Footwork vs Coach-fed

For a family-wise $5\%$ level, use

$$
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),15}
=
t_{0.99167,15}
=
2.69
$$
:::

::::

---

## Badminton: Bonferroni Results {.badminton-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display:grid; grid-template-columns: 0.56fr 0.44fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 16px 16px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.notebox .calc-left style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.56em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni calculation</span>

Because each group has $n_i=6$:

$$
SE
=
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
$$

$$
SE
=
\sqrt{
4.90
\left(
\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}
\right)
}
=
1.28
$$

The Bonferroni margin is:

$$
t^*SE
=
2.69(1.28)
=
3.44
$$

So each interval is:

$$
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)\pm3.44
$$
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.53em; line-height: 1.06; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Pairwise Bonferroni intervals</span>

| Pair | Bonferroni CI | Decision |
|---|---:|---|
| Static - Footwork | $-5.00\pm3.44=(-8.44,\,-1.56)$ | Different |
| Static - Coach-fed | $-6.50\pm3.44=(-9.94,\,-3.06)$ | Different |
| Footwork - Coach-fed | $-1.50\pm3.44=(-4.94,\;1.94)$ | Not different |

<br>

An interval that does **not** contain 0 gives evidence that the two population means differ.
:::

::: {.thinkbox style="grid-column: 1 / span 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.12; padding: 14px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>

Static targets is lower than both Footwork + serve and Coach-fed targets.

Footwork + serve and Coach-fed targets are **not** clearly different because their interval contains 0.
:::

::::

## Visual: Badminton Drill Accuracy Scores

```{r}

                 levels = c("Static targets", "Footwork + serve", "Coach-fed targets"))

badminton_means <- badminton |>
  group_by(drill) |>
  summarise(mean_score = mean(score), .groups = "drop")

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = badminton,
    x = ~drill,
    y = ~score,
    type = "box",
    name = "",
    boxpoints = FALSE,
    whiskerwidth = 0.55,
    line = list(color = "rgba(0,77,64,0.85)", width = 2.1),
    fillcolor = "rgba(200,230,243,0.38)",
    hovertemplate = "Drill: %{x}<br>Score: %{y}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_markers(
    data = badminton_means,
    x = ~drill,
    y = ~mean_score,
    marker = list(size = 9, color = plot_cols$red, symbol = "circle",
                  line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = "Drill: %{x}<br>Mean score: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "Serve-target accuracy after two months of drill training",
    x_title = "Badminton drill program",
    y_title = "Accuracy score out of 40",
    height = 390,
    margin = list(l = 70, r = 25, t = 60, b = 70)
  ) |>
  layout(
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Accuracy score out of 40",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 20,
      dtick = 2,
      range = c(18.5, 31.5)
    )
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.68em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-top: 10px;"}
The **red dots** show the group means. Static targets is clearly centered lower, while the two higher drill programs overlap more closely.
:::

## Example: Phone Case Drop-Test Costs {.phone-case-example}

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.90fr 1.10fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 8px 16px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.54em; line-height: 1.07; padding: 9px 12px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A device lab tests four phone case designs. After a standardized drop test, it records repair cost.

ANOVA rejects the equal-means hypothesis.

| Case | Mean repair cost |
|---|---:|
| Clear | 75.88 |
| Slim | 87.50 |
| Wallet | 98.50 |
| Rugged | 113.00 |

The ANOVA error estimate is $MSE=17.89$, with $v=28$ error degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.stat-card .calc-left style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.07; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni setup</span>

There are $m=\binom{4}{2}=6$ pairwise comparisons.

Bonferroni uses:

$$
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),28}
=
t_{1-0.05/12,28}
=
2.839
$$

For equal sample sizes $n_i=8$:

$$
SE=\sqrt{17.89\left(\frac18+\frac18\right)}=2.115
$$

Bonferroni margin: $2.839(2.115)=6.00$.
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.53em; line-height: 1.07; padding: 8px 12px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Question</span>

Which phone case designs have different population mean repair costs?

A pair differs if its Bonferroni interval does not contain 0.
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.53em; line-height: 1.08; padding: 8px 12px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
The Bonferroni margin is 6.00. So a pairwise difference must be more than 6 dollars away from 0 to be clearly different at the family-wise 5% level.
:::

::::

---

## Phone Case: Bonferroni Results {.phone-case-results}

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 0.82fr 1.18fr; gap: 20px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.67em; line-height: 1.20; padding: 13px 16px;"}
<span class="label">How to read the table</span>

Each interval estimates a difference in population mean repair cost.

If 0 is not in the interval, that pair of phone case designs has different mean repair cost.
:::

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.65em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px;"}
Here, all Bonferroni intervals avoid 0, so all pairs differ.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
| Pair | Difference | Bonferroni CI |
|---|---:|---:|
| Clear - Slim | -11.63 | $(-17.63,\,-5.62)$ |
| Clear - Wallet | -22.63 | $(-28.63,\,-16.62)$ |
| Clear - Rugged | -37.13 | $(-43.13,\,-31.12)$ |
| Slim - Wallet | -11.00 | $(-17.00,\,-5.00)$ |
| Slim - Rugged | -25.50 | $(-31.50,\,-19.50)$ |
| Wallet - Rugged | -14.50 | $(-20.50,\,-8.50)$ |
:::

## Visual: Phone Case Mean Repair Costs

```{r}
#| echo: false
case_data <- data.frame(
  cost = c(75,70,82,78,76,80,72,74,
           80,92,85,88,90,84,95,86,
           100,96,102,98,95,101,97,99,
           110,115,105,120,112,118,108,116),
  type = factor(rep(c("Clear", "Slim", "Wallet", "Rugged"), each = 8),
                levels = c("Clear", "Slim", "Wallet", "Rugged"))
)

case_summary <- case_data |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarise(mean_cost = mean(cost), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    n = 8,
    MSE = 17.8884,
    df_error = 28,
    se = sqrt(MSE / n),
    t_star = qt(0.975, df_error),
    lower = mean_cost - t_star * se,
    upper = mean_cost + t_star * se
  )

plot_ly(
  data = case_summary,
  x = ~type,
  y = ~mean_cost,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  marker = list(size = 11, color = plot_cols$red,
                line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
  error_y = list(
    type = "data",
    symmetric = FALSE,
    array = ~upper - mean_cost,
    arrayminus = ~mean_cost - lower,
    color = "rgba(0,77,64,0.75)",
    thickness = 1.8,
    width = 10
  ),
  customdata = ~cbind(lower, upper),
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "Case: %{x}<br>",
    "Mean repair cost: %{y:.2f}<br>",
    "95% CI: [%{customdata[0]:.2f}, %{customdata[1]:.2f}]",
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "Mean repair cost with 95% confidence intervals",
    x_title = "Phone case design",
    y_title = "Mean repair cost",
    height = 390,
    margin = list(l = 78, r = 25, t = 60, b = 70)
  ) |>
  layout(
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Mean repair cost",
      zeroline = FALSE,
      showline = TRUE,
      fixedrange = TRUE,
      linecolor = plot_cols$border,
      gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.07)",
      tickmode = "linear",
      tick0 = 70,
      dtick = 10,
      range = c(68, 122)
    )
  )
```

::: {.thinkbox style="font-size: 0.68em; line-height: 1.18; padding: 12px 15px; margin-top: 10px;"}
The **red dots** show the sample mean repair cost for each phone case design. The vertical lines show ordinary 95% intervals for the group means before applying the pairwise Bonferroni comparison.
:::

## Check in R: Pairwise Comparisons {.compact-r}

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Badminton drill example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

score <- c(19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25,
           24, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30,
           26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31)

drill <- factor(rep(c("Static", "Footwork", "Coach-fed"), each = 6))

anova(lm(score ~ drill))
pairwise.t.test(score, drill,
                p.adjust.method = "bonferroni",
                pool.sd = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Phone case example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false

cost <- c(75,70,82,78,76,80,72,74,
          80,92,85,88,90,84,95,86,
          100,96,102,98,95,101,97,99,
          110,115,105,120,112,118,108,116)

case <- factor(rep(c("Clear", "Slim", "Wallet", "Rugged"), each = 8))

anova(lm(cost ~ case))
pairwise.t.test(cost, case,
                p.adjust.method = "bonferroni",
                pool.sd = TRUE)
```
:::

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A one-way ANOVA with $k=4$ groups has a significant p-value. How many pairwise mean comparisons are possible?
::::

- 3
- [6]{.correct data-explanation="The number of pairwise comparisons is choose(k, 2). With k = 4, choose(4, 2) = 6."}
- 8
- 16

## Final Checklist

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Before calculating ANOVA</span>

- Identify the response variable.
- Identify the grouping variable.
- State $H_0:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k$.
- Check independence, Normal errors, and equal variance.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">After calculating ANOVA</span>

- Fill in df, SS, MS, and $F^*$.
- Use the right-tail F p-value.
- Reject only when the p-value is small.
- If ANOVA rejects, use pairwise comparisons.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** ANOVA compares several means by asking whether between-group variation is large compared with within-group error variation.
:::
